To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we can determine the parameters of a gravitational-wave signal from an inspiral with a spinning, non-precessing component, and that for an observation of a spinning, preccesing binary we can determine the sky position of a source to an accuracy better than 100 square degrees.

we can determine the parameters of an inspiral source of a black hole-neutron-star binary with a spinning, non-precessing component to an accuracy of 10-20%, and for an observation of an object with sufficient spin and at least two detectors, the accuracy in the determination the sky position is tens of square degrees.
the sky position and the binary orientation are estimated with an accuracy of the order of several tens of square degrees and several tens of degrees respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
parameter estimation for gravitational wave signals from inspiraling compact binaries.
the analysis of gravitational waveforms, and the estimation of the physical parameters of compact binary systems.
the analysis of the gravitational waveforms of inspiral signals from compact-object binaries, with the goal to extract information about the physical properties of the sources.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

we have shown that the parameter estimation of spinning compact binary inspirals can be carried out in a robust and reliable way, and that the accuracy of the estimation is higher than what has been claimed before.
the parameter estimation for spinning inspirals is feasible with the current generation of ground-based detectors.
we can determine the distance to the binary with 20% accuracy, and the orientation of the orbital plane with 10-20 degrees.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we can measure the parameters of a black hole-neutron-star inspiral to an accuracy that allows us to identify the source as a black hole-neuron star merger, and to locate it on the sky with an accuracy sufficient to allow electromagnetic follow-up observations.
the accuracy of parameter estimation is better than what was thought before, but still not sufficient for a confident identification of the source.
the inspiral signal from binary black holes or binary neutron star inspirals can be used to localize the source with a precision of a few square degrees.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spin of the black hole can be measured with a precision of about 0.1.
the spin and precession information can be extracted from the data, and that the spin of the neutron star can provide a powerful handle for the determination of the source orientation.
, in the presence of sufficient spin, the sky localization of the binary can be improved by a factor of 10 to 100 compared with the case of a nonspinning binary.
